Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association (MMA)
In Opposition to LD 710, An Act to Expand Access and Reduce Barriers to Access to Naloxone Hydrochloride and Other Opioid Overdose-reversing Medications
March 17, 2025 ________________________________________________________________
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, my name is Amanda Campbell, and I am submitting testimony in opposition LD 710 on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC).
Municipal officials support the many programs and services available to their residents who are suffering from addiction or who are in the process of recovery.
However, despite the continued provision for requiring municipal consent, municipal officials oppose the expansion of the statute that allows for overdose reversing medications to be stored in a "wall-mounted box or other visible container" to include vending machines as a mechanism for medication distribution on municipal property. While this provision would provide a different type of low-barrier access to these medications, municipal officials feel that the current statute already provides for that access.
Thank you for your consideration of the municipal perspective on this important topic. Please feel free to contact any member of the LPC or the MMA Advocacy team with any questions relating to municipal operations.

Good morning, Chair Ingwersen and Chair Meyer, and Members of the Health and Human Services Committee,
My name is Annika Moore, and I am the Advocacy Team Leader at Preble Street. Preble Street's mission is to empower people experiencing problems with homelessness, housing, hunger, and poverty and to advocate for solutions to these issues.
Preble Street strongly supports LD 710, An Act to Expand Access and Reduce Barriers to Access to Naloxone Hydrochloride and Other Opioid OverdoseReversing Medications. This bill focuses on expanding access to opioid overdose-reversing medications, reducing barriers to Narcan distribution, and providing legal protection for individuals and organizations that respond to opioid-related overdoses.
Studies show that Narcan and other opioid-reversing medications are critical, especially when it comes to harm reduction. Preble Street's Health Services program conducted a study that was funded through the Maine Health Access Foundation to gather insight from people who use drugs on needs and services to reduce fatal and non-fatal overdose. This grant specifically hired people with lived experience and peers to develop a survey alongside Preble Street Health Services staff. Of 102 survey respondents, 21 were housed independently, 15 were in permanent supportive housing, 38 were in a shelter, and 28 were unsheltered.
43% of survey respondents reported not having easy access to Narcan outside Monday - Friday business hours. However, when stratifying data, not including those in 24/7 shelters or permanent supportive housing programs and only accounting for people experiencing unsheltered homelessness or in independent living, that number increased to 60% of people reporting not having easy access to Narcan outside Monday - Friday business hours. Contrasting these barriers to the potential of 24/7 Narcan locations, 96% of survey respondents said 24/7 Narcan locations would help them access Narcan. In open-ended questions, answers relating to increased Narcan access were the second most common response. In discussions with people with lived experience participating in the grant and survey respondents, vending machines were a commonly suggested intervention in achieving 24/7 Narcan access, which is part of the proposed legislation.
Due to these community findings, Preble Street urges you to pass LD710 because it will increase accessibility to life-saving medication, allow community-based organizations to distribute Naloxone without being subject

Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services Testimony in Support of L.D. 710, An Act to Expand Access and Reduce Barriers to Access to Naloxone Hydrochloride and Other Opioid Overdose-reversing Medications
By Heide Lester on behalf of EqualityMaine

March 17, 2025
Dear Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Committee on Health and Human Services,
My name is Heide Lester, and I am the Deputy Director of EqualityMaine, which has been advocating on behalf of Maine's LGBTQ+ community since 1984. We strongly support the expansion of access to naloxone hydrochloride and other opioid overdose-reversing medications and the mitigation of barriers.
LGBTQ+ people have higher rates of substance use and substance use disorders compared to non-LGBTQ+ people: LGB adults are nearly twice as likely as heterosexual adults to experience a substance use disorder,1 and transgender people are almost four times as likely as cisgender people to experience a substance use disorder.2 Higher rates of substance use disorder are often exacerbated by social stigma, discrimination, and the pressures of minority stress. But, the increased availability of naloxone helps many people, including and especially vulnerable communities, and removing barriers to effective interventions and respecting the health and dignity of people who use drugs are essential components of a comprehensive strategy to tackle overdose rates.
Naloxone distribution programs are a key strategy for reducing overdose fatalities; with access to naloxone, lay responders, such as people who use opioids, their friends and family, and social service providers can prevent overdose death. Overdose education programs prepare lay responders to respond to overdose by providing education about risk factors for opioid overdose, signs of opioid overdose, naloxone administration, and aftercare procedures and can help improve readiness and confidence in responding to someone who may be experiencing an overdose. However, specialized training is not needed to use naloxone.3 Additionally, stigmatizing beliefs about naloxone and the people who use it have proven to negatively impact training goals among naloxone training participants.4 While people who use substances are

LD 710 - An Act to Expand Access and Reduce Barriers to Access to Naloxone Hydrochloride and Other Opioid Overdose-reversing Medications
Testimony in Support March 17, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, my name Matt Marston and I am the Chief Pharmacy Officer for Northern Light Health. I am here today providing testimony speaking in support of this bill. Northern Light Health member organizations include 10 hospitals located in southern, central, eastern and northern Maine, 8 nursing facilities, air and ground ambulance, behavioral health, addiction treatment, pharmacy, primary and specialty care practices and a state-wide home care and hospice program. Ninety three percent of Maine's population lives in the Northern Light Health service area. Northern Light Health is also proud to be one of Maine's largest employers with more than 10,000 employees statewide.
Expanding access to naloxone hydrochloride to the community is a goal that Northern Light Health has supported since Title 22, �2353 went into effect. We have expanded access through our primary care clinics, community outreach programs, hospital ED and acute care settings, as well as through our outpatient retail pharmacy locations providing over one thousand kits at no cost to our patients each year. Despite these efforts and the flexibilities that were provided by this statute, barriers remain.
Healthcare providers are held to numerous standards above and beyond those of public health and community programs that restrict the ways in which we can provide medications. CMS Conditions of Participation, Joint Commission standards, and Board of Pharmacy Regulations all dictate the methods in which pharmacies and other healthcare providers must handle the dispensation of drug products. In consultation with the Joint Commission and Northern Light Health legal counsel, we are proposing additional amendments to the existing legislation to extend immunity protections to healthcare works for administering over the counter (OTC) naloxone in the event of an overdose as well as to specifically identify OTC naloxone as the more common product presentation today that should not be subject to the same rigorous standards as prescription only products as called for by CMS and the Joint Commission. It is our hope that through these changes we can further expand upon what we have built for access at Northern Light Health as well as the medical community at large.
Northern Light Health would be happy to work with the committee to address any follow-up questions or concerns related to this bill.

LD 710, An Act to Expand Access and Reduce Barriers to Access to Naloxone Hydrochloride and Other Opioid Overdose Reversing Medications

March 17, 2025

Senator Ingwerson, Representative Meyer, esteemed fellow committee members, thank you for hearing LD 710, an Act to Expand Access and Reduce Barriers to Access to Naloxone Hydrochloride and Other Opioid Overdose Reversing Medications

I am presenting this bill on behalf of the department, and Katherine Coutu from the Office of Behavioral Health will be testifying after me.

At its core, this bill facilitates access to life-saving opioid reversal medications, through a variety of small changes to Title 22 Chapter 556-A, section 2353:

1. Strengthens immunity protections for Good Samaritans.

2. Permits a municipality to dispense an opioid overdose-reversing medication from a vending machine.

3. Removes the training requirement. Naloxone hydrochloride ("Narcan") is an ideal life-saving medicine for a Good Samaritan who has no formal medical training. It is highly effective, immediately active, easy and safe to administer, and rather inexpensive. When administered to someone suffering an overdose of opioids, it very well can save their life. If administered by accident to someone who was mistakenly thought to be experiencing and overdose, it causes no harm.

4. Generalizes statute from naloxone to "any opioid overdose reversing medication." Naloxone is the most well known of these, but it is not alone and

2
likely new medicines will be developed. It therefore does not make much sense to limit statute to this one particular medicine. Thank you very much for hearing this bill, and I look forward to fruitful discussions as a committee.
